kurz: Consulting Deep Dive, part 11: digital, tech and AI, from QuantumBlack and BCG X to Accenture, and the routes into tech and start-ups
A research version of Claude fails to prove the Riemann hypothesis but pushes a decades-old bound from 41.6 to 67.2 per cent
The Nasdaq 100 briefly touches bear-market territory, then claws back most of the loss as chips stay weak

meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 11: digital, tech and AI, from QuantumBlack and BCG X to Accenture, and the routes into tech and start-ups
meldungen.text:
For most of its history, strategy consulting sold slide decks and judgement. That model is being rebuilt around technology, and the clearest measure is money: BCG reported revenue of 14.4 billion dollars for 2025, its 22nd consecutive year of growth, and said that tech- and AI-focused services now account for more than 40 per cent of the total. Every large firm now runs a technical arm alongside its classic generalist practice, and for someone entering the industry in 2027 the choice between the two tracks matters more than it did five years ago.

At BCG, that arm is BCG X, launched in late 2022 by merging the firm's data science, digital build and venture units. By BCG's own account it employs about 3,000 technologists, designers and entrepreneurs in roughly 80 cities. Its staff build products and AI systems for clients rather than merely recommending them, and the firm has been experimenting with hybrid "forward deployed" roles that sit between engineer and consultant. McKinsey's equivalent is QuantumBlack, the analytics firm it acquired and turned into its AI practice; its leadership describes the goal as people who are strong consultants and strong engineers at the same time. Industry reporting this year describes McKinsey, BCG and PwC alike racing to hire engineers while retraining the rest of their staff in AI.

Accenture sits at the other end of the spectrum: far larger, more delivery-heavy and closer to an IT services company, with a strategy unit on top. It illustrates the harder side of the shift. According to recent coverage it is letting go of staff who cannot be retrained for AI-era delivery, while spending heavily on acquisitions such as a reported 4.1 billion dollar deal for the industrial cybersecurity firm Dragos.

The work itself is changing shape as well. Management Consulted, which published two new rankings of AI transformation firms for 2027 this week, argues that genuine enterprise AI transformation means redesigning the operating model rather than plugging tools into the existing one, and that it rarely starts with the CEO: more often a single function head, such as a chief procurement officer, wants that function to work differently. Its companion analysis warns that the market has become crowded and that most firms sound identical; the ones that stand out define clearly what they will not do.

For exits, the tech track is the most direct bridge into product and start-up roles. A Management Consulted dataset of 2,393 LinkedIn-verified job moves by current and former MBB consultants in the first quarter of 2026, reported by Poets and Quants, found that 52.3 per cent went to private companies, mostly venture- or private-equity-backed firms; 4.7 per cent of moves were into CEO roles, 4.2 per cent to partner and 3.7 per cent to founder. The authors concede the data undercounts people in stealth start-ups. Former consultants who moved told Business Insider that the pull is speed: start-ups can react faster in a market that changes monthly. Typical landing points from BCG X or QuantumBlack are product management, AI strategy or chief-of-staff roles at scale-ups, and later founding a company.

The trade-off is real. The tech arms recruit heavily from computer science, data science and engineering, and a pure strategy generalist may find the path to private equity slightly shorter from the classic track. But for a candidate who combines business training with quantitative depth, the technical units are the fastest-growing door into the industry.

meldungen.titel: A research version of Claude fails to prove the Riemann hypothesis but pushes a decades-old bound from 41.6 to 67.2 per cent
meldungen.text:
An Anthropic employee set a research version of Claude a deliberately absurd task: prove the Riemann hypothesis, the conjecture about the zeros of the zeta function that has resisted mathematicians since 1859 and carries a million-dollar Millennium Prize. Unsurprisingly, the model did not solve it. Along the way, however, it improved a related mathematical bound that had been stuck at 41.6 per cent for decades, lifting it to 67.2 per cent. Two mathematicians at Anthropic checked the result, and a formal proof was produced in Lean, a language in which a computer verifies every logical step.

The scale of the run is as striking as the result. Over a day and a half, Claude coordinated 60 subagents, which executed some 2,400 shell commands, wrote hundreds of Python scripts, checked thousands of known zeros of the zeta function and downloaded 54 papers from the arXiv preprint server. The subagents were set to review one another's proofs. The run consumed about 31 million tokens.

Mathematically, Claude combined recent work by Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya and Turnage-Butterbaugh with a paper by Enrico Bombieri from 2000. It built a function space with a Weil-type quadratic form, separated its positive- and negative-definite subspaces and derived an inequality for the rank of that form. The decisive move, according to the write-up, was to treat the whole space at once instead of first reducing the quadratic form to diagonal form.

The episode has a curious human footnote. Claude was initially sceptical of its own chances, presumably because training had taught it the limits of language models on open research problems. The only human input reported was encouragement along the lines of "keep going" and "believe in yourself", after which it delivered.

Some caution is in order. The German coverage comes largely from outlets in a content partnership, the figure of "160 years" in some headlines is loose (the hypothesis dates from 1859, so 167 years), and an improved bound is a contribution to number theory, not a breakthrough on the conjecture itself. Independent review by mathematicians outside Anthropic has not yet been reported. Still, a model that plans and verifies a multi-day research project, with a machine-checked proof at the end, is a marked step beyond summarising papers.

It also lands in a busy week for the company: Anthropic has just introduced Claude Ship, which automates pull requests from code review through fixes to approval, while its shares, only days after listing, closed on Wednesday at 82.79 dollars, a whisker below the 83-dollar IPO price.

meldungen.titel: The Nasdaq 100 briefly touches bear-market territory, then claws back most of the loss as chips stay weak
meldungen.text:
Wednesday brought the sharpest intraday swing on Wall Street in weeks. Shortly after the opening bell the Nasdaq 100 fell as much as 4.7 per cent, leaving it 20 per cent below its early-October record, the conventional threshold of a bear market. By the close it had recovered most of the ground and finished only 0.6 per cent lower. Of 65 AI-related stocks tracked by the tech outlet Trending Topics, 36 closed in the red, with an average loss of 0.8 per cent, against 4.1 per cent before the bell.

The recovery was uneven. Semiconductors remained the weak spot, dragged by the scandal around Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang and stricter US export rules for AI hardware. The 15 chipmakers in the sample lost 3.3 per cent on average, after SK Hynix and Samsung had already fallen 11.1 and 9.9 per cent in Asia. Nvidia closed 3.9 per cent lower at about 149 dollars, having been down 9.1 per cent; Micron, at one point 13 per cent down, ended 4.5 per cent lower. Software turned positive: IBM rose 3.3 per cent and Salesforce 2 per cent, while Oracle lost 5.1 per cent. Anthropic recovered from a morning fall of almost 10 per cent to close at 82.79 dollars, just below its 83-dollar issue price.

Macroeconomic data added to the nerves. The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, the PCE price index, rose 3.8 per cent year on year in October, as expected, but core inflation came in at 3.3 per cent, slightly above forecasts. Futures markets now price a roughly 98 per cent chance of a quarter-point rate rise in December, which would mark a turn towards tighter policy. The new US tariff proposals (see US Politics) weighed on sentiment too.

Europe fared worse than New York, because its markets closed before the rebound: the DAX lost 1.3 per cent and Vienna's ATX 3.1 per cent. The VIX volatility index rose 5.2 per cent to around 28, a level that signals real stress. Bitcoin slipped back below 60,000 dollars.

What comes next is complicated by the calendar. US exchanges are closed today for Thanksgiving and trade only a shortened session on Friday; thin volumes can amplify moves in either direction. Measured against last Friday the AI basket is still up 3.8 per cent, but it trades on average about 42 per cent below its highs for the year, and the so-called neoclouds, which rent out GPU capacity, about 70 per cent below.

meldungen.titel: Washington proposes a new wave of tariffs on China, the EU and 12 other economies, this time on firmer legal ground
meldungen.text:
The Trump administration has announced a fresh round of import tariffs aimed at many of America's largest trading partners. The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) published proposed duties on goods from China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, India, Switzerland, Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Cambodia and Bangladesh, together with lengthy reports on how each jurisdiction's trade practices allegedly harm American commerce. China faces the highest rate, up to 40 per cent, followed by Vietnam at up to 35 per cent; most others face 20 or 25 per cent.

The legal basis is the key change. The White House opened these investigations in March, after the Supreme Court ruled that the "Liberation Day" tariffs of April 2025, imposed under emergency powers, were illegal. The new levies rely instead on Section 301, which lets the USTR retaliate against specific foreign trade practices. Many Section 301 tariffs from Trump's first term survived through the Biden administration, which is why economists see them as more durable, although legal challenges are expected. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the duties would "level the playing field for American workers", accusing partners of targeting manufacturing and suppressing wages.

The practical impact may be smaller than the headline numbers suggest. Caps agreed in earlier deals effectively reduce several rates: the European Commission stressed that tariffs on EU goods remain limited to the 15 per cent agreed last year and said it would examine the justification, while South Korea called its expected 15 per cent "more than a decent outcome". Capital Economics argued that the new duties largely replace tariffs announced in the summer and cover a limited range of goods, so the effective tariff rate should rise only marginally. Japan called the move "regrettable"; Vietnam said the rate did not reflect bilateral cooperation. Separately, Washington proposed a 10 per cent tariff on Brazil, which President Lula's office rejected outright.

Nothing takes effect immediately. The proposals must pass public consultation and possibly hearings, and the duties are not expected before next year. The announcement also shows that the president is pressing on with his signature policy despite his party's poor result in this month's midterm elections.

meldungen.titel: Germany: CDU MPs propose a "Respekt-Rente" to keep penalty-free early retirement for low earners, but put no figure on the cost
meldungen.text:
The decision. In the coalition dispute over the so-called "Rente mit 63", three CDU/CSU MPs, deputy parliamentary leader Johannes Winkel, social policy spokesman Marc Biadacz and Pascal Reddig, head of the party's young MPs, presented a two-page compromise on Wednesday, according to ARD; parliamentary group leader Thorsten Frei is reported to back it. People with 45 contribution years who earned at most 70 per cent of average pay would keep retiring without deductions. Above that threshold, regular deductions would apply only to the pension points earned above the line. Child-rearing and care periods would still count. Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants the cabinet to adopt the core of the pension reform before Christmas.

The case made. The authors argue that low earners disproportionately work in physically and mentally demanding jobs, and that the model makes early retirement "targeted and socially fair" while keeping it affordable for contributors and younger generations. The CDA, the party's labour wing, called it a "very good compromise". The sharpest criticism came from within the Union: Christian von Stetten, head of the parliamentary Mittelstand group, called it a "capitulation" before the need for a comprehensive reform.

The numbers. The government's pension commission recommended abolishing penalty-free retirement after 45 years outright in its report of 23 June 2026, one of 33 proposals. The pension is substantial: roughly 30 per cent of all new old-age pensions go to "particularly long-term insured" people (Deutsche Rentenversicherung, Bertelsmann Stiftung, DIW). ZDF, citing pension insurance data, put new recipients without deductions at about 269,000 in a year; in 2025 around 926,000 people drew an old-age pension for the first time. A DIW study for the Bertelsmann Stiftung (June 2026) estimated that full abolition would save the pension insurance about 10.4 billion euros per birth cohort (modelled on the 1957 cohort), or about 9.5 billion net for the state after roughly 860 million euros of lost health, care and income tax revenue, and would keep about 125,000 full-time equivalents in work, assuming retirement is delayed by ten months on average. The regular retirement age currently stands at 66 years and four months; the early route allows retirement up to two years sooner.

Reality check. The data support the premise that the scheme is large and costly. The claim that low earners are concentrated in strenuous jobs is plausible and consistent with an Austrian Arbeiterkammer analysis published the same day, which finds low earners less likely to reach retirement in work, but the paper cites no German figures. The DIW finds the scheme is used mainly by people with stable careers, not only those in physically demanding work, which cuts in both directions. Crucially, the proposal contains no costing: how many future retirees fall below the 70 per cent line, and how much of the 9.5 billion euro saving would survive, is unknown. Whether a long working life deserves reward regardless of income is a value judgement the numbers cannot settle.

Evidence rating: Thinly grounded. The size of the scheme is well documented, but the proposal's central promise of affordability rests on no published estimate of what the income threshold would save.
